extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, production staff, and manuscript editors
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and practical guidance for producing and managing academic journal content in print and electronic formats, aimed at editors, publishers, and production staff. Covers front/back matter, metadata, versioning, supplemental content, design, and format-specific considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal home page content and features
rubrics_metrics.description: A journal’s home page should provide information and resources not tied to a particular issue, updated as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes staff members; history of the journal and sponsoring society; extensive information for authors about preparation and submission of electronic text, tables, math, art, and other files (e.g., video files or large data sets); links to publisher/society/home pages and field databases; individual and institutional subscription forms; site license agreement and registration forms; links to tables of contents for previous issues; lists of articles scheduled for upcoming issues or links to articles published electronically ahead of upcoming issues; a journal-specific or broader search engine; information about indexing and abstracting services; society meeting abstracts and membership information; special services for subscribers (e.g., email TOC distribution); links to related products (books, newsfeeds, blogs); and mail-to links for manuscript submission/review, subscriptions, advertising, permissions, technical issues. (See also 1.105.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Table of contents content and electronic linking
rubrics_metrics.description: The table of contents (TOC) should list essential issue and article-level bibliographic data and provide direct links and format options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TOC should include journal title (or special issue title and guest editors), date/month/season/year, volume and issue numbers, article titles and authors, and page ranges (or starting page). May contain section titles or subheads and list review articles, book reviews, commentaries, editorials, or other items. Should include articles published electronically-only or direct readers to the website for such a list. Electronic TOC should provide links to each format of each item and to article summaries (abstracts and other viewable info). Full articles freely available should be labeled. Include options for downloading citations to individual articles. (See figure 1.11; also 14.5.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Information for contributors
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should provide author-facing guidance about preparation and submission of manuscripts and editorial policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information can vary from a brief sentence to several pages and may include a statement of editorial policy. If not in printed cover pages, these components may appear in front or back matter; printed journals often provide a brief version and point authors to the electronic version for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal acknowledgments, announcements, and calls for papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Periodic front-or-back-matter items should acknowledge reviewers, announce awards/conferences, and call for papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These may appear in preliminary pages or at the end of an issue. Supplements or special issues should include title page with supplement title, guest editors, source/sponsorship information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errata handling and linking
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic journals should link errata bidirectionally with the corrected articles and document small post-publication changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errata in print may appear in front or back matter. Electronic journals should provide two-way links from errata to the articles containing the errors; articles themselves should indicate or link to relevant errata. TOC entries for original articles should contain links to errata. Small online corrections (broken images, typos) should be accompanied by a note indicating the changes and when made. (See also 1.112.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction content and linking
rubrics_metrics.description: Retractions must identify the retracted work and provide a brief explanation and linking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction should include the title of the retracted article, full author list, volume and issue where it appeared, and a brief (usually two to three sentences) explanation for the retraction (e.g., plagiarism or data falsification). Electronic retraction should link to the retracted article; the article should include a link to the retraction and a notice that it has been retracted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal article metadata requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate and complete metadata must be incorporated into records shared with libraries and content providers to facilitate discovery and access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metadata includes journal title and ISSN, volume and issue number, author and affiliations, article title, page range, publication date, article DOI, format (print, HTML, PDF, e-book), language, content (abstract and keywords), subject headings, access rights, funding sources, and other details. Metadata may be recorded using standard XML-based syntax (e.g., Dublin Core, JATS) and can include elements to track versions through proofreading and testing stages or to facilitate citation linking. (See also 1.93, 1.117.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstracts and keywords guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstracts and keywords play a crucial role in discovery and must follow journal requirements and conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstracts are typically a few hundred words or less, supplied by the author, appear at the start of the article, and are generally made available as stand-alone items; thus they normally do not contain cited references, figure callouts, or direct links to the article. Content is important for influencing readers’ decisions; some journals have strict structural requirements for research abstracts. Abstracts are not usually required for letters, reviews, or similar materials. Keywords supplement abstracts to increase visibility for search engines and indexing; keywords normally repeat key terms from title/abstract/text but may include synonyms or variations and can use controlled vocabularies (e.g., MeSH). (See also 1.92, 1.111.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of articles and other journal components
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals publish a variety of content types beyond standard articles, each treated and labeled appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Components include research articles, review essays, survey articles, symposia, brief reports, letters to the editor, book reviews, book notes, announcements, calls for papers, errata, notes on contributors, and ancillary materials. Abstracts are considered part of articles (see 1.93).

rubrics_metrics.name: Article first-page (front-matter) information
rubrics_metrics.description: Each article should present core bibliographic and author information prominently on the first page or near the top in electronic versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An article should include the article title, author name(s), and copyright line. Depending on journal needs, include author affiliation(s), relevant financial interests/conflicts, correspondence/reprints address, submission and acceptance dates, electronic publication date (common in sciences), an abstract and keywords, acknowledgment note, and sometimes an editor’s note. A section heading (Articles, Review Essay, Symposium) or subject heading (e.g., Medical Microbiology) may appear above the title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-references and navigational links within articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic articles should include internal links and links to outside resources to facilitate navigation and access to supplementary materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Links can point to tables, illustrations, reference list entries, notes, sources cited in reference lists, field-specific indexes/databases, supplementary materials not in print. Articles may include menus to move to other article sections or formats (PDF), issue TOC, previous/next article, journal home page, search options, cited-by data, and citation/sharing tools; displays may include thumbnail versions of tables/illustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subheads and sectioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles may be divided into sections and subsections with appropriate heading levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subheads (and sub-subheads) are used as needed; the number of subhead levels may vary by article. See general guidance on headings (1.55-58).

rubrics_metrics.name: Book and journal reviews formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Book reviews have prescribed heading information and variable length determined by the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review headings should list the book author, book title, place/date of publication, publisher, number of pages (including front matter), and price; series title if applicable. The reviewer’s name typically appears at the end of the review or follows the heading; reviews may have their own title with reviewer name following. Book notes use the same heading form but are much shorter and reviewer initials may be used. Journals may also publish reviews of journals, films, or other media and lists of books received for review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Announcements content
rubrics_metrics.description: Announcements cover notices of conferences, calls for papers, award nominations, research subjects, and employment opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers should allocate space for such notices in appropriate sections of the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributor information and indexing
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic contributor information should appear with articles and be included in metadata; publishers may provide contributor indices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributor affiliations typically appear at the head of the article or on the first page and are included in article metadata and online summaries. Publishers may offer an index of past contributors or a special section with contributor information (publications, fields).

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters to the editor treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters may be minor components or prominent features depending on discipline and journal practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters may be published irregularly or only online; in some scientific journals, letters are regular and prominent, often with replies, and may include equations, tables, and figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorials and special-issue introductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorials announce significant changes or provide introductions to special issues and may be authored by editors or invited contributors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorials may explain change of editor, policy/style changes, added/dropped features, or redesign. Special issues usually include an introduction by guest editors with heading 'Editorial' or 'Introduction' and the editor’s name at the end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright line content and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Each substantive article should carry its own copyright line containing bibliographic and rights information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copyright line usually appears at the bottom of the first page (below footnotes) or at the head for full-text electronic articles and contains: (1) issue information (journal title, volume/issue numbers, publication date, inclusive page numbers), (2) the copyright notice (symbol, year, name of copyright owner—publisher or sponsoring society), and (3) a series of numbers (Copyright Clearance Center code) with ISSN, year, volume/issue, article number, and per-copy photocopying fee payable via CCC. Some journals include the article’s DOI in the copyright line. Note CCC relations with international agencies and that fees apply only to copyrighted material, not public domain. (See 4.55-57, 4.97.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication history and dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic publication dates and, where applicable, submission and acceptance dates should be included to provide context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For articles published electronically before print, the electronic publication date should appear as part of the article’s history in both print and electronic versions—on the first page or near the head. Some journals also include date received and date accepted; these dates help interpret timing, especially in fast-moving sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserving historical/contextual materials for articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should consider making back-issue front matter and ancillary materials available to preserve historical context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because content is often offered as individual articles, publishers who wish to preserve context should provide covers, front matter, and other ancillary materials from the original issue along with articles so that readers can assess historical context such as editors, sponsors, or advertisers relevant to interpreting a work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tables: multiple presentation formats and linking
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables can be presented as images, searchable hypertext, or machine-readable data allowing reuse and linking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table footnote citations should link to table footnotes for navigation in large tables. Links enable readers to move from text to tables and between tables. Very large tables may be published online only; if print version exists, both versions should make differences explicit. For full discussion see 3.47-88.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrations, multimedia, and differing print/electronic content
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic formats allow higher-resolution images, color, audio, video, and more illustrations than print; differences must be noted explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic articles may display thumbnails linked to larger images, include audio components, videos and animations. Color can be used freely though color accuracy varies by display. Differences between print and electronic content should be noted explicitly in both formats. See 3.3-46 for discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source citation systems and documentation style
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals use particular documentation styles (notes or author-date) which identify the journal's character and must be applied consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes (prevailing in humanities) may be footnotes or endnotes (heading 'Notes'); author-date citations (sciences/social sciences) are parenthetical keyed to a reference list at the end. Some scientific journals use numbered references cited by reference number with references listed alphabetically or in order cited. See Chicago chapters 14 and 15 for preferred systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linking citations to references and external resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic citations should link to reference list entries and potentially to outside resources to facilitate navigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full-text electronic articles and enhanced PDFs typically link text citations to references or bibliography entries and allow readers to move from text to cited item and back. Reference lists and bibliographies may link to resources outside the article (e.g., cited articles or external indexes/databases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Print volume indexes versus electronic indexed searches
rubrics_metrics.description: Indexing practices differ: some journals publish printed indexes while many rely on searchable bibliographic databases and search engines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the end of a volume some journals publish an index listing authors, article titles, and books reviewed; detailed subject indexes are rarer and in sciences have been largely superseded by field-specific bibliographic databases (e.g., PubMed). Readers accessing articles via databases may need subscriptions or paywalls for full-text access. (See also 1.92, 1.93.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Version of record and version control practices
rubrics_metrics.description: When the electronic version is the version of record, any changes to files after electronic publication must be documented and tracked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The print version may include only a subset of electronic material. Document any post-publication changes; errata that concern an article in the same issue should specify the date of electronic publication. Use systems like CrossRef’s CrossMark to track versions, corrections, and retractions. Consult NISO/ALPSP JAV recommendations for best practices. (See 1.112.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprints, in-press, and published-ahead-of-print distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate between preprints, versions submitted to journals, in-press items, and final edited electronic articles published ahead of print.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may circulate drafts or post to preprint servers; journals may post 'in press' or 'forthcoming' items accepted but not edited—these should not be confused with final edited electronic articles published ahead of print. Some journals use continuous publishing, releasing final articles individually independent of print issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental content availability and archival responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplemental materials (multimedia, large data sets, supporting information) must be listed in print and made available electronically with assurance of ongoing accessibility and archival standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplemental content should be explicitly noted in print versions and made accessible online. Publishers must provide content in a way that ensures permanence and accessibility regardless of whether electronic version is version of record; implement standard practices for document structure/markup and supplemental media inclusion/identification and consult standards bodies (ISO, Digital Library Federation) for archival practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal design principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A journal’s physical, visual, and editorial design should be simple, flexible, visually pleasing, and easy to read, and determined at the journal’s founding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design specifications should cover categories of text (title, author, text, heads, subheads). Electronic design shared across journals on the same parent site has additional medium-based considerations. Manuscript editors and production staff must fit items of an issue into the overall design. Long-running journals may redesign typographically; minor style changes common in electronic formats to accommodate technology changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial style and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: A journal’s editorial style governs typographic and usage conventions and contributes to identity through consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style covers when to use numerals or percent signs, treatment of abbreviations or special terms, organization of tables, etc. Consistent design and style let substantive content stand out and reduce typographic distractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic workflows and structured markup
rubrics_metrics.description: Electronic publishing workflows should use markup to identify document parts and enable conversion across formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many publishers use electronic workflows with XML (e.g., JATS) to facilitate conversions to PDF, e-book, HTML, or apps. Markup identifies parts of a work (titles, subheads, text, illustrations) so content can be repurposed and rendered appropriately in different contexts. Publishers not using standards can develop customized workflows but should ensure consistent tagging. An online supplement to the manual offers further overview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overview of electronic publication formats (PDF, e-book, HTML, apps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different electronic formats have distinct properties and use-cases that inform how content is prepared and presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PDF preserves fixed-layout and is nearly identical to print; text can be searchable and hyperlinks added; supports embedded multimedia though rarely used. E-book formats (EPUB, similar) support reflowable text, images, linked TOC, and navigational tools suited to page-at-a-time reading and bookmarking. HTML is ideal for multimedia, complex tables, extensive hyperlinks, and user interaction in browsers. Apps allow specialized presentations and are adaptable to mobile devices or third-party bookshelf apps; offer the widest possibilities for presenting content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional features and platform testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional features available depend on format and publisher implementation; must be designed with user interaction in mind and tested across reading environments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For PDF/e-book, features depend on reader applications and devices; for web and apps, features are determined by publisher design and rarely vary per issue. Custom web presentations/apps may require design and implementation from scratch. Publishers must assess functionality with an understanding of content and user interaction and have a system for checking content in each environment in which it may be read. (See 2.137-40.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Navigation and search in electronic publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective navigation (search, linked TOC, cross-references) is essential for electronic works; readers expect fast, context-sensitive searching and pathways between items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Searchable PDFs may be enhanced with linked TOC and internal links; EPUBs include linked TOC and internal links encoded in package. Web-based publications/apps must cater to readers consulting smaller pieces out of order and expecting many cross-references. Context-sensitive keyword indexing enhances search; links to popular content or cited-by statistics help readers know where others land. (See 16.7.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Link management and permanence in electronic formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers must manage hyperlink quantity, relevance, and permanence to avoid reader irritation and broken links; prefer permanent identifiers for external links.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no cost to following a hyperlink if a user can step back and forth, but too many links or irrelevant/broken links are harmful. Limit external links in PDFs/e-books to internal cross-references or permanent identifiers (e.g., DOI). Web content is more flexible; some links can be checked/generated programmatically (e.g., related titles by metadata matching). Publisher-created links require maintenance and often cost; consider using DOIs or other permanent identifiers for outside resources and programmatic checks for link integrity. (See 2.34.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Front and back matter adaptation for electronic formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional front/back matter should be rethought for electronic reading contexts and made accessible without hindering core content navigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PDF and most e-book formats retain traditional front matter and order. Web readers prefer quick access to core content; ancillary elements (prefaces, copyright, author info) can be demoted and made accessible via margins, home pages, 'about us' links, site maps, help menus, and search. Copyright info should usually be included with each subdocument and help should be available from any part of the publication. TOC may be a significant driver of top-level navigation for web-based works.
